title: Maple, Hazel, and the Lost Map
markdown:
The moon was a sliver of pale cheese, and Lily slept with her breathing soft and even. Outside her window the night belonged to leaf-rustle and the occasional distant hoot.

Teddy Maple’s fur was the colour of warm toast, a little worn from countless hugs, button eyes holding a quiet knowing glint. He listened more than he spoke. Squirrel Hazel lived in the grand oak just beyond the glass: quick as a shadow, tail a perpetually curious question mark, ginger fur and darting eyes always ready for the next thrill.

When the house grew silent — old wood creaking, an owl far off — a whisper no louder than a moth’s wing reached Maple’s stitched ear. Willow the robin perched on the sill, chest puffed with importance.

“Maple,” she chirped, voice like tiny silver bells. “There’s a parcel. Very urgent. For Bartholomew, the shy dormouse, deep in the Old Beech Woods. He’s been waiting all week. New thimble-sized reading glasses. He can’t see his books without them.”

Maple’s button eyes widened. Bartholomew was a gentle sort, reserved, living alone in a snug burrow with books and the rustle of his own thoughts. A nighttime delivery meant the glasses mattered. Maple imagined small paws wringing, pages unread.

Hazel, who had been dozing on the highest branch, perked up, ears swiveling. “Parcel? Woods? Moonset?” Her tail twitched. “Count me in. Adventure calls.”

Maple nodded, a slow thoughtful movement that rippled his stuffing. “It’s a bit of a journey. The woods can be tricky at night, especially with something as vital as Bartholomew’s sight. The moon is already sinking. If we don’t get there soon, he’ll be plunged into darkness until dawn.” He was not precisely afraid. The thought of getting lost, of fumbling the delivery, did prickle at his stuffing. He smoothed his fur, a nervous habit.

Hazel bounced on her branch. “We’ll be fine. You’ve got steady paws. I’ve got speedy feet. Lily always says we’re a great team.”

Maple slipped from the bed, plush paws silent on cool carpet. Hazel scampered down the oak and met him by the garden gate, eyes gleaming. Their mission: the Old Beech Woods, where ancient trees whispered to the wind and last year’s leaves carpeted the ground in faded colours.

The allotments were easy: sleeping flowerbeds, garden gnomes that seemed to wink. At the old wooden fence a rather flustered rabbit hopped toward them, spectacles slipping down his long nose. Professor Hops, chief mapmaker for the Woodland Committee, renowned for a brilliant mind and an equally brilliant talent for misplacing his sense of direction.

“Ah, Maple. Hazel.” He panted, fumbling a rolled parchment that looked suspiciously like a large damp leaf. “You’ve come for the map. Bartholomew’s parcel, very important. This,” he unfurled it, narrowly missing Hazel’s nose, “is the absolute most accurate up-to-the-minute chart of the fastest route. Guaranteed.”

Squiggly lines. Spidery script as if written by a nervous beetle. “Follow the Whispering Stream, then left at the Grumpy Stone. Easy peasy.” He adjusted his spectacles with a triumphant sniff.

Hazel paused. She had a knack for finding things, honed by years of burying and unearthing acorns. She held up a second, older map, acquired earlier from a wise owl named Archimedes in the tallest pine. “This one says go right at the Grumpy Stone, and follow the Giggle Brook. It says it’s quicker after a dry spell, and it hasn’t rained in days.”

Maple looked from one map to the other, stitched seams creasing. The woods seemed to sigh, privy to the dilemma. “That’s the curious thing about maps. They don’t always agree. And sometimes the most important paths aren’t the ones most clearly drawn.”

They pressed on with Professor Hops’s leaf-map. What they thought was the Whispering Stream sounded more like a gurgle. Trees grew taller, branches interlacing like bony fingers. The air smelled of damp earth, decaying leaves, and the sharp clean scent of pine. A gruff cough. A grumpy grumble.

From behind a thicket of ferns whose fronds drooped like tired old men emerged Saoirse Badger, known for her solitary nature and a rather short temper, especially when naps were disturbed. She squinted, small eyes like shiny pebbles. “Lost, are we? Always with these silly nocturnal errands. You’ll never find Bartholomew this way. This path,” she gestured, “leads to the old hollow oak. Echoes and dust bunnies. Waste of time. And a nuisance to my slumber.”

Saoirse was usually grumpy because she felt overlooked. Decades of digging and foraging had given her a vast knowledge of the woods, but no one asked her for directions. She had tried once — an elaborate explanation involving stars and the scent of foxgloves — and no one had listened. She had retreated into solitude.

“But our map,” Hazel began, pointing to Professor Hops’s creation, voice a little shaky.

Saoirse scoffed, pebbles rattling in a tin. “That buffoon’s map? He drew it during a sneeze. The only sensible way is to follow the moss on the north side of the trees. Nature’s compass. Reliable, unlike some rabbits I could mention. Now be off before I lose my temper completely.” She huffed back into the ferns, muttering about the general incompetence of mapmakers.

The parcel was important. The moon, that sliver of pale cheese, sank lower. Professor Hops pointed one way, the owl another, Saoirse a third. Hazel wanted the path that seemed most direct. Maple felt the familiar urge to pause, to consult every scrap, to avoid any possibility of a mistake. He hesitated between caution and her impatient energy.

“We can’t possibly follow all of them,” Hazel said, tail flicking. “One of them must be wrong. Professor Hops’s map just led us to a grumpy badger and a dead end.” She nudged the leaf-map; it snagged on a thorny bramble and tore. “Oh, bother.”

Maple felt a pang for not insisting on Archimedes’s map, or even Saoirse’s moss. A sharp thorn snagged his plush ear. Consequence of mingled indecision and haste.

“This is all wrong,” he said, voice low. “We can’t just pick one, and we certainly can’t ignore all of them. They all have a reason. Professor Hops maps the streams, the flow of water. The owl maps the ancient paths. And Saoirse knows the moss, and how it grows where the sun doesn’t reach.”

They stood. Damp earth. Sharp tang of torn brambles. Then Maple noticed: the path Saoirse had grumbled about, the one to the hollow oak, was lined with moss thickest on one side. Beyond it, a faint gentle murmur of a stream — not quite a whisper, not a roar. A soft musical sound.

“Look. The moss is thickest toward that sound. And that sound isn’t exactly the Giggle Brook, and it isn’t the Whispering Stream either. It’s in between.”

Hazel peered. “As if all the maps are partly right, pointing to slightly different versions of the same place. Like looking at the same tree from different angles.”

“Precisely.” Warmth spread through Maple’s stuffing. His caution had been paralyzing him; Hazel’s impulsiveness, wonderful for new paths, sometimes missed details. “We’ll follow the moss on the north side, which Saoirse mentioned. That will lead us toward a stream. Then we listen. If it sounds like the Giggle Brook, we follow that. If it sounds more like the Whispering Stream, that way. All the clues. All the perspectives.”

They set off on mossy ground, following sturdy moss-covered trees. Soon a small bubbling brook: a musical gurgle that did sound a little like laughter.

“A bit like the Giggle Brook,” Hazel whispered.

“And flowing from the direction Professor Hops vaguely indicated,” Maple added. “A blend of all their directions.”

They followed the brook as it wound. Around a bend the woods opened into a small clearing bathed in fireflies — tiny lamps blinking in a silent ballet. Cool sweet air, night-blooming jasmine. The brook a lullaby. For a while they only stood and looked. The lights did not hurry them. They simply were, a thousand tiny stars dancing just for two travellers with a parcel.

A little way off, at the foot of a grand ancient beech whose bark was a tapestry of moss and lichen, a small cosy burrow. A tiny warm light flickered within.

“Bartholomew,” they whispered together.

Maple carried the parcel like a jewel. They knocked on the acorn-shaped door. A small whiskered face peered out, hope and apprehension mixed.

“We have your parcel,” Maple said.

The dormouse’s whiskers quivered. He took the brightly wrapped package with trembling paws. “Thank you. New thimble-sized reading glasses. My old ones broke last week. I couldn’t see to read. I was so worried they wouldn’t arrive before the moon set, because then it would be too dark for the postman robin to see the path from the village.”

They looked at the sky. The moon was dipping, pale light weakening, long dancing shadows. They had made it.

Bartholomew put on the spectacles with a delicate touch. Magnified eyes sparkled. “You are the kindest friends a dormouse could ever ask for.”

They turned for home. Quiet satisfaction, warmer than any bedtime blanket. Confusion, conflicting advice, a mildly perilous badger — solved by listening, by combining Maple’s thoughtfulness and Hazel’s quick wit, by trusting what they knew together.

Dawn painted the east in rose and gold. The woods felt familiar now. Maple did not lecture himself about preparedness. He simply walked beside Hazel, parcel delivered, stuffing settled, the moss still dark on the north sides of the trees as if Saoirse’s compass had been waiting all along.
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing night-time woodland adventure for older children
